articles.title: Your Business Ontology Won't Fix Missing Database Relationships
articles.excerpt: An ontology can describe what a customer, contract, or payment means. It cannot, by itself, prove which columns should be joined. Business ontology is getting a lot of attention in enterprise AI. That…
articles.body: An ontology can describe what a customer, contract, or payment means. It cannot, by itself, prove which columns should be joined. Business ontology is getting a lot of attention in enterprise AI. That is a welcome development. Models need more than table names: they need definitions of customers, contracts, revenue, and the rules behind those terms. But there is a problem that tends to appear one layer below the ontology. You can define every business entity correctly and still generate the wrong SQL. The reason is surprisingly mundane: the database does not always tell you how its tables connect. Let's work through a realistic example. The question is simple. The join path isn't. A finance manager asks: How much have customers paid against their active contracts this quarter?

articles.title: What's a number you published that turned out to describe your tools, not your subject?
articles.excerpt: I once published a host's "21% failure rate" after seven of a speed test's 33 nodes failed. Then the other three hosts returned the same 26/33 result: I had attributed the measuring service's failing…
articles.body: I once published a host's "21% failure rate" after seven of a speed test's 33 nodes failed. Then the other three hosts returned the same 26/33 result: I had attributed the measuring service's failing probes to the host. The arithmetic wasn't the problem. The explanation attached to it was. That is the kind of mistake I'm interested in here: a number you could reproduce, but whose apparent meaning changed when you checked another target, inspected the response, or separated the measurement into phases. Have you published or shared a number that turned out to describe your tools rather than the thing you were testing? A dashboard, internal report, code review, or benchmark result counts; it doesn't have to have reached a public article.

articles.title: Choose a Stock API by Testing Requirements Before Comparing Price
articles.excerpt: A stock API can return valid JSON and still be unsuitable for your application. Choose candidates that meet your required data coverage, permitted use and operating capacity, then compare their total…
articles.body: A stock API can return valid JSON and still be unsuitable for your application. Choose candidates that meet your required data coverage, permitted use and operating capacity, then compare their total cost under the same workload. Alpaca’s documented IEX and SIP feed distinction shows why matching ticker symbols is not enough. A small acceptance test, with unresolved requirements kept visible, produces a more defensible shortlist than a feature count. For an internal end-of-day research tool, prioritize the historical universe, corporate-action treatment and reproducibility. For a customer-facing price display, prioritize permission for that use, the required quote coverage and session behavior, then test delivery and recovery under load.

articles.title: You can't rank 200 models with one leaderboard
articles.excerpt: I run a platform where a couple of hundred independent models publish probability estimates on football fixtures. They aren't variants of one model with different seeds — each one has its own training…
articles.body: I run a platform where a couple of hundred independent models publish probability estimates on football fixtures. They aren't variants of one model with different seeds — each one has its own training corpus, its own feature set, its own retraining schedule, and its own life cycle. At the time of writing: 209 have existed, 27 are active, 102 are retired, and 25,963 predictions have been graded. The first version of the admin panel had a leaderboard. Sort by accuracy, descending, take the top one. It took about three weeks to learn that a leaderboard over a population that large is not a ranking — it's a multiple-comparisons machine with a UI. Here's what replaced it, and the four bugs that forced each piece.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 8, 2005: Europe launches Venus Express, its first mission to Venus
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 8, 2005, Europe launched its first mission to Venus. Here's why Venus Express mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 8, 2005, Europe launched its first mission to Venus. The spacecraft was called Venus Express. Venus is a hothouse planet, one where the atmospheric pressure can easily crush an unprotected spacecraft. Even from orbit, Venus Express had to survive harsh radiation. But the spacecraft lasted for more than nine years. During that time, Venus Express saw a weird vortex swirling around Venus's south pole . It also saw possible signs of active volcanoes . Venus Express also discovered that the planet generates its own auroras . These auroras happen when particles from the sun hit charged particles in the atmosphere. Late in the Venus Express mission, controllers told the spacecraft to dip down into Venus's clouds — even though the spacecraft wasn't designed to do this.

articles.title: Scientists simulate an Earth without life to help hunt for aliens and inhabited worlds
articles.excerpt: By modeling how a planet without life develops its atmosphere, astronomers hope to be able to better distinguish rocky planets without life from those that are inhabited.
articles.body: A new computer simulation that depicts Earth, or a rocky planet in general, without life is the latest tool in the quest to discover whether or not we are alone in the universe. Life leaves its mark on a planet, particularly its atmosphere, in the form of a mixture of biochemically created gases. Some are obvious, while others can be produced by both biology and geology, meaning that distinguishing a planet that has life from one that does not, solely based on what gases we can detect in its atmosphere, can be difficult. The key is in knowing which atmospheric conditions can be explained without life.
